AI disruption, a deep pool of private sellers, strategic industry alignment and rich premiums for scale point to a broader deal cycle ahead. Despite relative softness in the M&A market in the third quarter of 2026, activity levels year to date remain elevated. Total volume is up 26% compared with the same time period in 2025, with a 22% jump in the number of deals valued above $10 billion. J.P. Morgan expects continued momentum for a broader M&A cycle. In the latest M&A report, we explore four forces shaping the market heading into the end of the year. Infographic showing year-to-date M&A activity: 26% increase in global M&A volume versus 2025, and 22% increase in deals over $10 billion year-to-date, illustrated with teal and orange upward arrows. AI has moved from concept to execution, becoming the central driver of deals and capital formation in 2026. Hyperscalers alone are expected to spend $650 billion on capex this year, and the figure is projected to exceed $1 trillion in 2027. The gap between leaders and laggards is widening. Just 20% of organizations capture roughly 75% of AI’s economic value. Rising cybersecurity threats add urgency. The result is dealmaking that extends well beyond conventional acquisitions. Companies are securing critical inputs such as compute and power through contracts and partnerships, buying differentiated capabilities like proprietary data and talent, and repositioning exposed portfolios through carve-outs and mergers. Minority investments and partnerships lead the way: AI-driven deals made up 54% of minority stake sales in the first eight months of 2026. For subscale companies, the rising cost of competing could make a sale or merger with a scaled operator increasingly attractive, accelerating future M&A deal flow. Roughly 6 million U.S. small and midsized businesses face ownership transitions by 2035 as founders retire, putting about $5 trillion in enterprise value in play. Simultaneously, sponsors are under pressure to return capital as 2026 marks the fourth straight year of below-normal sponsor liquidity. Around 32,000 portfolio companies worth roughly $4 trillion sit unsold in the U.S., and implied holding periods have stretched to seven years versus the historical average of five. With a near-record $2 trillion in dry powder waiting to be deployed, the conditions are in place for a high-velocity M&A cycle. Sponsors are increasingly turning to structured exits including continuation vehicles, minority stake sales and net asset value financing. Infographic highlighting two figures: $1T projected hyperscaler capital expenditures in 2027, and approximately $4T of unrealized value across roughly 32,000 unsold sponsor-backed companies. Government policy is steering capital toward strategic sectors — defense, shipbuilding, bioscience, energy, semiconductors and next-generation networks — by working to lower investment risk. Shipbuilding is one such example. The White House’s February 2026 maritime action plan calls for rebuilding U.S. commercial and defense shipbuilding, including encouraging partner countries to invest in domestic shipbuilding. The plan includes financing support, tax incentives and public-private partnerships. The U.S. is encouraging partner countries to invest in domestic shipbuilding; as a result, South Korea has committed $150 billion to the effort Similarly, strategic alignment on 6G has spurred policy coordination between the U.S. and 25 other nations representing about 55% of global GDP. Members of the group have signed a pact to coordinate rollout, with standards and trials expected between 2027 and 2029. The pact aligns points of contact between nations as the 6G buildout progresses, encourages both industry and academia engagement, and aims to strengthen both supply-chain transparency and security standards on the road to commercial deployment of next-generation networks. The bigger M&A tailwind may be the knock-on effect: large strategics applying their competitive advantages to a broader opportunity set, from automakers moving into defense to industrials expanding into software. Investors continue to reward scale. Market value is concentrating in a handful of the largest companies, where increased scale and higher growth are translating into near multi-decade-high valuation premiums and multiple spreads. Valuation premiums are near all-time highs, and they show up across both company size and geography. Within the U.S., the median S&P 500 company trades at 12.6x EV/EBITDA, versus 10.4x for the small-cap S&P 600. In Europe, multiples are lower: large caps on the STOXX 200 trade at 11.0x and the FTSE 100 at 8.7x. The U.K.'s mid-cap FTSE 250 trades at just 6.6x, roughly half the S&P 500 multiple. Growth earns a premium too: the gap between high- and low-growth firms is 7.9 turns on the S&P 500, compared with 6.2 on the STOXX 600. These gaps cut two ways. Scaled acquirers, especially in the U.S., have a highly valued currency to pursue larger deals, including cross-border targets that look inexpensive by comparison. Meanwhile, subscale and lower-valued companies face mounting pressure to combine to close the gap. Geopolitical turmoil, higher oil prices, persistent inflation and rising interest rates may delay some transactions and widen valuation gaps. But these factors don’t change the structural forces driving the cycle. AI will continue to drive acquisitions, partnerships and capability add-ons across every industry. Sponsor backlogs and the ownership transfer wave will broaden private M&A, while strategic activity will likely increase in policy-driven critical sectors. Large strategics that paused activity in the third quarter represent pent-up demand that could re-emerge as headwinds subside. Capital is pouring into the sport, which has become a strategic asset class with a flourishing investment ecosystem. The 2026–2027 football season in Europe recently kicked off — and investors are hoping to score big. This is especially true as the “beautiful game” has evolved beyond a traditional spectator sport and into an attractive asset class. Major football clubs in Europe are highly sought after because they offer various opportunities for value creation, thanks to their engaged consumer base and lucrative media rights. According to Deloitte, the European football market generated a record €40.2 billion in revenue over the 2024/2025 season, crossing the €40 billion threshold for the first time. Additionally, Football Benchmark reports that the aggregate enterprise value of Europe’s top 32 football clubs has nearly tripled since 2016, significantly outpacing general inflation and traditional financial indices. Today, investors are pouring capital into European football through various avenues, from M&A to structured equity and debt financing. What are the key investment trends to watch, and how is the market maturing? The rise of multi-club ownership in European football Multi-club ownership (MCO) occurs when a single investor holds controlling or minority stakes in multiple football clubs across different leagues. It is one of the most significant investment trends in European football today, offering advantages such as: While MCO can create a conflict of interest, it is managed through strict rules — for instance, governing bodies like the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) enforce rules stating that two clubs controlled by the same owner cannot play in the same tournament. Currently, over 120 top-division football clubs in Europe — around 16% of the total — are part of an MCO network. This includes almost half of those in the “Big Five” leagues, namely: Prominent examples include RB Leipzig and FC Red Bull Salzburg (part of the Red Bull franchise), as well as Manchester City FC and Girona FC (under City Football Group). In December 2024, Everton FC became part of an MCO portfolio when it was acquired by privately held consortium The Friedkin Group, which also owns AS Roma and AS Cannes. J.P. Morgan facilitated the process, providing an initial bilateral credit facility of £130 million to fund the acquisition. Thereafter, the firm raised £350 million of debt to help refinance Everton FC’s new stadium, which opened in February 2025 — a key milestone under the club’s new ownership. The growing role of private capital and private wealth Like The Friedkin Group, private capital players are increasingly acquiring stakes in European football clubs, attracted by under-monetized commercial revenues and rising franchise valuations. More than a third of clubs in Europe’s “Big Five” leagues now have backing from private equity, venture capital or private credit firms. In August 2022, private equity firm RedBird Capital Partners purchased AC Milan from hedge fund Elliott Management for €1.2 billion, with the aim of expanding the club’s commercial presence globally. J.P. Morgan advised AC Milan on the deal, which marked the largest ever football transaction in Italy. Ultra-high-net-worth individuals are also headlining major buyouts. Take, for instance, British businessman Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s purchase of a 25% stake in Manchester United in December 2023, which was the largest ever transaction in the EMEA sporting world. J.P. Morgan advised Sir Ratcliffe on the roughly £1.25 billion deal. The firm was also instrumental in advising Italian-American businessman Rocco Commisso, the former chairman of Mediacom, in his acquisition of Serie A club ACF Fiorentina back in 2019. Transactions such as these are a testament to J.P. Morgan’s holistic sports investment banking ecosystem, with the firm’s Private Bank servicing high-net-worth individuals interested in investing in sports and the Corporate and Investment Bank facilitating the deals. “By partnering across the firm, we’re able to drive successful outcomes and deliver exceptional value for our clients,” said Eric Menell, global co-head of Sports Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. “By partnering across the firm, we’re able to drive successful outcomes and deliver exceptional value for our clients.” Global co-head of Sports Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan Stadium redevelopment has become a defining capital investment theme in European football. Many clubs are modernizing aging infrastructure to meet stricter UEFA standards. Some are also reimagining stadiums as mixed-use entertainment platforms that can host non-sporting events — increasing both project complexity and the scale of financing. At the same time, investor interest in sports infrastructure assets such as stadiums and arenas has increased dramatically as valuations have risen. “Part of that is due to the value of live content, which consumers are gravitating toward,” said Tim Self, head of Public Finance and Infrastructure Direct Lending at J.P. Morgan. “Also, unlike in the U.S., where new franchises are still being formed as certain leagues expand into new markets, there’s effectively a fixed supply of sports assets in Europe. As more wealth is created, there’s a lot of money chasing a limited number of top-tier sports assets — and that’s driving valuations to ever higher levels.” J.P. Morgan has structured numerous stadium financings in Europe, supporting clients with capital and arranging syndication across both loan and bond markets. The firm is the leading global arranger and agent for sports and entertainment infrastructure transactions, and has $3.5 billion in capital currently committed for stadium, arena and related infrastructure debt financings globally. A case in point is Real Madrid CF’s five-year renovation of its Santiago Bernabéu stadium, which transformed the iconic venue into a state-of-the-art entertainment hub complete with a retractable grass pitch. J.P. Morgan was deeply involved throughout the project’s lifecycle — from navigating court challenges to structuring financing terms. The firm served as sole placement agent for all four financing rounds, securing multiple ‘A’ category ratings and raising a total of €1.5 billion. In the same vein, FC Barcelona is currently refurbishing its Camp Nou stadium, with works expected to be completed by 2028. The new design is expected to increase the stadium’s capacity from 99,000 to more than 105,000 spectators, as well as add a VIP ring and a sweeping panoramic screen. J.P. Morgan spearheaded the $1.6 billion capital raise, acting as financing bank, structuring agent and placement agent. Both the Santiago Bernabéu and Camp Nou are slated to host matches during the 2030 FIFA World Cup, showcasing the outcomes of these transactions on a global stage. “As more wealth is created, there’s a lot of money chasing a limited number of top-tier sports assets — and that’s driving valuations to ever higher levels.” Head of Public Finance and Infrastructure Direct Lending, J.P. Morgan From blockbuster deals to behind-the-scenes transactions While mega-deals continue to dominate headlines, investors are also supporting European football clubs behind the scenes. “Football clubs today sit on a broad range of valuable but often illiquid assets,” said Taoufik Bounhar, global head of Credit Solutions Trading at J.P. Morgan. “Our Global Credit Solutions Trading team works alongside our Banking, Public Finance and Private Bank partners to deliver bespoke financing and liquidity solutions, helping clubs and owners unlock value from player transfer-related cash flows, as well as media, sponsorship and other contractual receivables. We also offer selected opportunities that we underwrite to our Alternative Credit investors — either through outright participation or synthetic risk-transfer structures — creating efficient capital solutions for clubs while providing investors access to differentiated credit investment opportunities.” In addition, J.P. Morgan offers European football clubs other solutions like debt structuring. For instance, following Chelsea FC’s takeover in 2022, J.P. Morgan structured an £800 million debt facility for the club’s new owners, investment consortium BlueCo. title: Will JPMorgan's Nigeria Expansion Bolster Its Growth Prospects? - TradingView
content: JPMorgan Chase & Co. JPM is advancing its expansion plans in Nigeria after the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) granted approval-in-principle to establish JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited. The move marks a significant step in JPMorgan’s efforts to deepen its presence in Africa’s largest economy and expand its corporate and institutional banking services. Can JPMorgan’s Nigeria Banking License Strengthen Its African Presence? The CBN granted approval-in-principle to JPMorgan on Oct. 23, 2026, allowing it to proceed with plans to establish a merchant bank in Nigeria. The development follows the bank’s reported deposit of 50 billion Nigerian naira (approximately $38 million) with CBN as part of its licensing process. The deposit represented a key regulatory requirement but did not guarantee approval. JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited is expected to expand the bank’s ability to serve Nigerian corporations and institutional clients. Its proposed activities include wholesale banking, capital markets and advisory services. The expansion could also create opportunities in lending, payments, trade finance and cross-border transactions. JPMorgan has maintained a representative office in Lagos for years. Establishing a locally licensed merchant bank would provide a broader platform to serve businesses and participate in Nigeria’s financial markets. The approval-in-principle represents only the initial stage of the regulatory process. JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited must complete the remaining requirements, including incorporation with the Corporate Affairs Commission and the necessary operational arrangements, before receiving authorization to commence business. The proposed Nigerian merchant bank also aligns with JPMorgan’s broader efforts to strengthen its African presence and capture corporate and investment banking opportunities across the region. The bank has reinforced its regional investment banking leadership through appointments covering sub-Saharan Africa, Kenya and Ivory Coast, reflecting its focus on expanding client coverage and strengthening relationships with businesses, governments and institutional investors. Nigeria’s position as a major African economy could make the proposed bank a valuable addition to JPMorgan’s regional operations. However, the scale of the opportunity will depend on regulatory approvals, client demand and the bank’s ability to establish profitable operations. In conclusion, JPMorgan’s planned entry into Nigeria’s merchant banking sector could strengthen its African presence and create new growth opportunities in corporate banking, capital markets, advisory services and cross-border financing. Nigeria’s sizable economy and growing demand for institutional financial services offer significant long-term potential. However, the expansion’s success will depend on securing final regulatory approval, attracting corporate clients and building profitable operations amid competition and market challenges. While the approval-in-principle marks an important milestone, its contribution to JPMorgan’s overall growth will ultimately depend on how effectively the bank converts its expanded presence into sustainable revenue and earnings.
